claims.claim: Le Guin (quoted by Garth) said there was no use trying to make a lexicon of Earthsea's languages, unlike Tolkien who in one sense wrote LOTR to give his languages speakers.
claims.source: John Garth, 'Ursula Le Guin, the language of Earthsea, and Tolkien' (blog)
claims.quote: No use trying to make a lexicon

claims.claim: Attebery (quoted by Garth) distinguishes her from Tolkien copyists as one who absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him and went her own direction.
claims.quote: absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him, and gone on in her own direction

claims.claim: Garth notes Le Guin called language invention 'the Secret Vice' after Tolkien's essay and counted LOTR among the three books she had re-read past counting.
In 'Dreams Must Explain Themselves' Le Guin named only the Shorter Oxford Dictionary and Follett's and Fowler's usage manuals as her tools (later Strunk & White).
claims.source: Stan Carey, 'How to see one's own world': Le Guin on writing style (Sentence first blog)

claims.claim: Carey foregrounds the essay's claim that style is the writer's way of seeing and speaking, and that the artist's hardest lesson is to see his own world and speak in his own words.
Margaret Mahy: in Earthsea language is not only the vehicle of the story but at times what the story is about, and Le Guin must find the right name before she can go on.
claims.source: Margaret Mahy, 'Speculations on the Earthsea Stories' (ursulakleguin.com)

claims.claim: The invented names carry conviction and inevitability, so the reader feels reminded of a land already known.

claims.feature: spoken voice in the reader's head
claims.claim: Mahy describes the reading experience as words on the page becoming a spoken voice in the reader's head — the storyteller addressing a reader-listener.
claims.quote: a spoken voice in the reader's head

claims.claim: Walton calls it one of the very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: succeeds in feeling like a legend

claims.claim: The narration passes easily from what people say and what isn't spoken of, from the distance of the fairy-tale teller to the very close, always sure where the teller stands.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: the distance of the teller of fairy-tales to the very close

claims.feature: told within the world, after the story
claims.claim: The story is told entirely within the world but after it, so the implied reader is assumed to know the great deeds referenced.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: told entirely within the world, but after the story

claims.claim: There is never a wasted word and all the words are right; it is like poetry and among the best books for reading aloud.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: There's never a wasted word, and all the words are right.

claims.claim: The names (Selidor, Iffish, Havnor, Osskil, Gont, Pendor) make the map memorable; the world is 'named and called up' from the first word.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: Le Guin is so wonderful with names

claims.claim: A world with much more in it than appears on the page — history, other countries — yet with a clear line drawn round it: 'only in silence the word'.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: a clear line drawn around it

claims.claim: Plotz (per Burt) calls the prose the antithesis of high-end video-game verisimilitude: it leaves blanks the reader fills, showing how often we fill things in.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of John Plotz, Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea (OUP 2023), Strange Horizons
claims.quote: the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude

verdicts.trueWording: No use trying to make a lexicon of Hardic
verdicts.note: Garth body text quotes Le Guin ('Dreams Must Explain Themselves', n.3): 'No use trying to make a lexicon of Hardic ... or of the True Speech; there's not enough in the books. It's not like Tolkien, who in one sense wrote The Lord of the Rings to give his invented languages somebody to speak them.' Quote and both limbs verbatim. verdicts.trueWording: absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him, and gone on in her own direction
verdicts.note: Quotation is on the page word for word and Attebery (The Fantasy Tradition in American Literature) does distinguish Le Guin from 'the Tolkien copyists' — but it is NOT Garth's text: it appears in a reader comment by David Bratman (28 Jan 2021), to which Garth replied 'Absolutely spot on!'. Attribution limb fails.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'quoted by Garth' — the Attebery quotation appears in a reader comment by David Bratman, not in Garth's post

verdicts.trueWording: lost count only with Dickens, Tolstoy, and Tolkien
verdicts.note: Secret Vice limb fully supported: 'In Always Coming Home (1985), Le Guin refers to language invention as "what an illustrious predecessor referred to as the Secret Vice" ... She meant Tolkien, whose essay "A Secret Vice"'. But the re-reading limb is misstated: Garth quotes her on LOTR — 'I reread a great deal, but have lost count only with Dickens, Tolstoy, and Tolkien' — three AUTHORS, not three books.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the three books she had re-read past counting' — the page names three authors (Dickens, Tolstoy, Tolkien), not three books

verdicts.trueWording: entire arsenal of tools: Shorter Oxford, Follett's and Fowler's manuals
verdicts.note: Carey quotes 'Dreams Must Explain Themselves' (1973): 'The Shorter Oxford Dictionary and Follett's and Fowler's manuals of usage are my entire arsenal of tools.' The 'only' limb is carried by 'entire arsenal'; the 1989 note supplies '(later Strunk & White)': 'Strunk and White's Elements of Style ... are my road-atlas to English.' Live URL 403 to curl; verified on Wayback raw capture 20260804234601id_.

verdicts.trueWording: Style is how you as a writer see and speak
verdicts.note: Claim carries no quote field, so graded on substance. Carey quotes 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie': 'Style is how you as a writer see and speak. It is how you see: your vision, your understanding of the world, your voice' and 'A good learner will finally learn the hardest thing: how to see one's own world, how to speak one's own words.' Carey does foreground it — it is the post's title. Page says 'one's own', not 'his own'.

verdicts.trueWording: at times, what the story is about
verdicts.note: Mahy, 'Speculations on the Earthsea Stories' on ursulakleguin.com: 'the language which is not only the vehicle by which the story is told, but is, at times, what the story is about.' Second limb is Le Guin to Mahy by phone: 'I must find the right name or I cannot get on with the story ... I cannot write the story if the name is wrong.'

verdicts.trueWording: names which had conviction and inevitability
verdicts.note: Mahy asks 'how she came to command names which had conviction and inevitability'; the reminded-of-a-known-land limb is her own reading experience in the preceding paragraph: 'searching the map ... I felt I was not so much acquainting myself with a new geography, but reminding myself of one that I already knew.' The causal join is the page's own ('Yet', contrasting with names that feel spurious).

verdicts.trueWording: words on the page translate into a spoken voice
verdicts.note: Mahy: 'the writer ... is not directing his or her story at a particular age group but at a particular sort of reader... a listener as well as a reader, for those words on the page translate into a spoken voice in the reader's head... and that reader-listener out there has an approximate connection to that first reader-listener.' Both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend
verdicts.note: Walton, Reactor, dated 2010-01-27: 'It's also one of the very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend.' Byline Jo Walton confirmed on page.

verdicts.trueWording: the distance of the teller of fairy-tales to the very close
verdicts.note: Walton: 'she passes easily from what people say, what isn't spoken of, the distance of the teller of fairy-tales to the very close. Whether she's inside or outside she has a tremendous grasp of the story she's telling and where the teller is standing in relation to it.' All three limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: told entirely within the world, but after the story
verdicts.note: Walton: 'The story is told entirely within the world, but after the story—the implied reader is assumed to know about the great deeds that are referenced.' Verbatim, both limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: There's never a wasted word, and all the words are right
verdicts.note: Walton: 'There's never a wasted word, and all the words are right. It's like poetry. This is one of the best books for reading aloud.' Verbatim including the poetry and read-aloud limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin is so wonderful with names
verdicts.note: Walton: 'I could draw the map from memory, and the reason for this isn't because it's an especially good map but because Le Guin is so wonderful with names—Selidor, Iffish, Havnor, Osskil, Gont, Pendor and the Ninety Isles.' The 'named and called up' limb is also verbatim: 'From the first word, from the names on the map, Earthsea is a very realised world, named and called up.' (Page's list also includes the Ninety Isles; claim's list is a subset, not stated as exhaustive.)

verdicts.trueWording: a world with a clear line drawn around it
verdicts.note: Walton: 'It's a world with a lot more in it than appears on the page—a history, of Elfarran and Erreth-Akbe, other countries, the Kargs, and it's a world with a clear line drawn around it—"only in silence the word".' Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude of a high-end video game
verdicts.note: Burt (Strange Horizons, review of Plotz): 'Leaving blank spaces for readers to see how well, and how often, we fill things in, Le Guin's prose is (Plotz writes) "the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude of a high-end video game" (p. 48).' Attribution to Plotz per Burt is explicit on the page; both limbs present.
